title: Age Disaggregation: From 5-Year Groups to Single Years
text: Many mortality data sources report rates abridged age groups (e.g. 30–34, 35–39, …\ldots, 90+). However, actuarial applications, life-table construction, population projections often require single-year--age rates. mortensor provides three disaggregation methods: Hyman + Kannisto: Monotone Hermite spline interpolation Kannisto logistic extrapolation old ages Natural + Gompertz: Natural cubic spline Gompertz log-linear extrapolation GAM-based: 2D GAM smoothing across age time, parametric blending tail method preserves group-average constraint (mean single-year rates within 5-year group matches original grouped rate) handles open age interval (90+) using parametric mortality laws.

title: Age Disaggregation: From 5-Year Groups to Single Years
text: Interior ages (30–89): Monotone Hermite spline interpolation (stats::splinefun(method = "hyman")) age-group midpoints. Hyman filter ensures monotonicity — rates increase age, expected adult mortality. Open interval (90+): Kannisto logistic model fitted: μ(x)=⋅ebx1+⋅ebx\mu(x) = \frac{\cdot e^{bx}}{1 + \cdot e^{bx}} provides realistic deceleration mortality increase old ages (“mortality plateau”). Group-mean correction: iterative multiplicative adjustment ensures average single-year rates within 5-year group matches original grouped rate.
code: fc_hk <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100,                       method = "hyman_kannisto")

title: Age Disaggregation: From 5-Year Groups to Single Years
text: Strengths: Guaranteed monotonicity; well-suited -cause mortality; Kannisto captures old-age deceleration Limitations: Can overly rigid cause-specific mortality non-monotone age patterns exist (e.g. breast cancer peaks middle age)

title: Age Disaggregation: From 5-Year Groups to Single Years
text: Interior ages (30–89): Natural cubic spline (stats::splinefun(method = "natural")) age-group midpoints. Natural splines allow non-monotone patterns, accommodating diseases peaked age profiles. Open interval (90+): Gompertz log-linear extrapolation: logμ(x)=α+βx\log \mu(x) = \alpha + \beta x fitted last age groups. assumes exponentially increasing mortality, appropriate causes age 80. Group-mean correction: iterative adjustment Hyman+Kannisto.
code: fc_ng <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100,                       method = "natural_gompertz")

title: Age Disaggregation: From 5-Year Groups to Single Years
text: Strengths: Flexible non-monotone age patterns; simpler extrapolation Limitations: May produce non-monotone patterns -cause mortality monotonicity expected; Gompertz can overestimate extreme ages

title: Age Disaggregation: From 5-Year Groups to Single Years
text: sophisticated approach, designed forecast surfaces temporal smoothness matters much age smoothness: Fit 2D GAM: mgcv::gam() tensor product smooths s(age,year)s(\text{age}, \text{year}) observed (training) data grouped ages. Predict single years: GAM predicts log(mx) single-year ages observed forecast years, extrapolating smoothly. Parametric tail blend: old ages, GAM prediction blended parametric model (Kannisto Gompertz) using logistic weight function: w(x)=11+e−(x−xopen)/τw(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(x - x_{\text{open}}) / \tau}} xopenx_{\text{open}} open-interval midpoint τ\tau controls transition width. Group-mean correction: Iterative correction ensures consistency.
code: fc_gam <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100, method = "gam")

title: Model Calibration, Selection, and Ensembles
text: Train/test split: last holdout_frac years (holdout_years) withheld evaluation. Smoothing: data$smoothed FALSE, smooth_mortality() called automatically. Tucker3 calibration: calibrate_tucker3() searches rank combinations CoDa Direct variants, selecting best (RA,RB,RC,ts_method)(R_A, R_B, R_C, \text{ts\_method}). model calibration: calibrate_all_models() evaluates Lee-Carter, FDM, StMoMo, RWD, ARIMA, ETS via expanding-window CV. Holdout comparison: compare_models() runs every calibrated model training set, forecasts holdout period, scores combined MASE (0.7 cell-level + 0.3 group-trend). Ensemble construction: top-kk models combined using inverse-MASE weights (optionally NNLS stacking).

title: Model Calibration, Selection, and Ensembles
text: Rolling-origin CV (rank_selection = "cv") trains expanding windows evaluates next hh years: CV procedure: rank combination, fit Tucker3 years [1,T0][1, T_0], forecast hh steps, score held-truth using chosen cv_metric. Roll forward: train [1,T0+1][1, T_0+1], forecast, score. Average scores across origins. Select ranks lowest average score. Given best ranks, compare ts_method ∈\{arima, ets, rwd}. default, scoring metric cell-level MASE (cv_metric = "mase"). can also use "mase_combined" (0.7 × cell + 0.3 × trend) "mase_trend" (trend ). See CV metric selection section .

text: Point forecasts alone insufficient mortality planning — actuaries, public health officials, pension funds need uncertainty quantification. mortensor provides two complementary approaches prediction intervals (PIs): Residual bootstrap: Resamples historical residuals simulates future time-series paths (fast, model-agnostic) GAM-Bayes posterior propagation: Draws GAM smoothing posterior, re-runs forecast pipeline draw, capturing smoothing uncertainty model uncertainty (slower, thorough) methods produce 95% prediction intervals optionally store full simulation array custom quantile extraction.

title: Prediction Intervals: Bootstrap and GAM-Bayes Methods
text: add_pi() main entry point. takes mort_forecast object (forecast()) augments PI bounds:
code: library(mortensor) data(example_mortality)  sm  <- smooth_mortality(example_mortality, method = "gam",                         covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L)) cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2, ensemble = TRUE) fc  <- forecast(cal, h = 10)  # Add prediction intervals fc <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

title: Prediction Intervals: Bootstrap and GAM-Bayes Methods
text: add_pi(), forecast object gains: fc$mx_lower: 3D array 2.5th percentile (lower 95% bound) fc$mx_upper: 3D array 97.5th percentile (upper 95% bound) fc$mx_median: 3D array median forecast fc$sims: 4D array [n_ages × h × n_groups × n_sim] (full simulations)
code: fc <- add_pi(   fc,   n_sim       = 500L,          # number of bootstrap/posterior draws   method      = "bootstrap",   # "bootstrap" or "gam_bayes"   cap         = 1.5,           # cap extreme simulations at cap × point forecast   calibration = NULL           # mort_calibration (needed for gam_bayes) )

title: Prediction Intervals: Bootstrap and GAM-Bayes Methods
text: bootstrap method resamples historical forecast residuals adds simulated future paths: Compute residuals: ex,t,g=log(m̂x,t,g)−log(mx,t,g)e_{x,t,g} = \log(\hat{m}_{x,t,g}) - \log(m_{x,t,g}) m̂\hat{m} -sample fitted values. Resample residuals: Draw BB bootstrap samples residual array (sampling years replacement, preserving cross-sectional dependence within year). Simulate time-series paths: Tucker3, re-simulate ARIMA/ETS fits B-mode using forecast::simulate(). Lee-Carter/FDM, simulate kt (period index) process. Reconstruct: Combine resampled residuals simulated paths produce BB forecast surfaces. Extract quantiles: 2.5th 97.5th percentiles across simulations give 95% PI.

text: Mortality data inherently multi-way: rates vary age, period, population group simultaneously. Univariate methods (Lee-Carter, ARIMA per series) ignore structure. mortensor models full age × period × group array jointly via Tucker3 decomposition, extracting low-rank patterns generalise better --sample.
